name: Dirty Pink
lede: Dirty Pink is a muted, slightly brownish rose first recorded by the 2010 xkcd color survey, where volunteers typed names at swatches on screen.

sections.title: A crowd name for a grayed pink
sections.body:
Dirty Pink has no listing in Ridgway, Maerz and Paul, or the ISCC-NBS charts; the only source on file is the xkcd color survey of 2010, where thousands of web users typed names at swatches and this one stuck [1]. The name follows a plain modifier grammar, *dirty* plus [[pink]], the same pattern behind [[dull-dark-purple|Dirty Purple]] and [[citronelle|Dirty Yellow]]: a base hue read as soiled or faded [1]. At hex #CA7B80 it measures lightness 60 and chroma 33 in LCH, and the nearest ISCC-NBS block reads as a dark pink [1].

Its closest named neighbors are [[old-rose|Old Rose]], 2.9 units off and duller, and [[dusty-rose|Dusty Rose]], 3.0 units off and almost the same; [[antique-pink|Antique Pink]] sits 3.0 units away and more vivid, and [[dusky-pink|Dusky Pink]] 4.1 units away and redder [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 0.19% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (46 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 15 [3]. In our archive it is rarer than 64% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 0.4% of the 1,674 paintings we have from that decade (7 paintings), 4.2 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light across its 15 appearances by lightness rank within the painting [3]. The earliest match dates to 1400, 610 years before the name's 2010 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a look-alike hue in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment or dye [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].
